TikTok, which has more than 2.3 billion downloads worldwide, has recently been valued between $30 billion and $50 billion.

But TikTok's China ties have attracted even more attention in recent months after the president and administration officials said earlier this month they're weighing a ban on the app. One possibility, raised by the White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow earlier this month, could see TikTok pull out of China and operate as an "independent American company."

The resulting uncertainty in TikTok's future has reportedly led ByteDance executives and investors to explore alternatives to avoid a US ban. Earlier this month, a group of ByteDance's US investors, including Sequoia Capital and General Atlantic, were looking into buying a majority stake in TikTok, according to The Information. But The Information reported Friday that those talks had failed, because of concerns that such a takeover "wouldn't pass muster with the Trump administration."

It's unclear what power Trump has to force a foreign company such as ByteDance to "divest" from TikTok's US operations. It's also unclear how TikTok or ByteDance will respond to an order, but Trump's move would represent an escalation in the administration's attacks on TikTok and other Chinese tech companies.

Not that you took exception to it, but to be clear about my point with the shock collar is that you want something that will temporarily debilitate and completely disorient the animal. You should never cause injury or pain as part of training (I'm sure you know this, but just so I'm clear for other readers). Striking a dog might be part of training, but the goal is to derail its train of thought to give negative reinforcement of the undesirable behavior and allow a chance for it to perform a desirable behavior that you can immediately reward. Striking should be just hard enough to get its attention, and never enough to cause pain. Too much, and the animal will hate you or fear you (and fear is probably the worse of the two). You want your dog to respect and follow you, never fear or hate (and those even more far apart for dogs than for humans).

Shocking is a little different, as the dog won't clearly connect the stimulus to you. The goal is the same (derail the train of thought, possibly provide an annoying stimulus, present it with a chance to perform desirable behavior), but there is a slightly wider range of stimulus available. At the low end, a very small shock is just enough for it to notice like a "funny feeling" and is often used in the place of oral feedback for deaf dogs. At the extreme end, which should be reserved only for the toughest cases, you want it to be the canine equivalent of you jumping into a freezing cold swimming pool - not at all harmful if done once by itself, but presenting an overriding negative input to the point of psychologically-generated physical debilitation and a complete realignment of your short term thought processes.

That's a lot of rambling stuff that you probably already know as much as you'd ever need to. But I don't want to leave some other reader with the impression that I'd advocate animal abuse.

I hooked a sawsall up to my mealworm sifting tray/colander. Game changer.
What does that do? My setup is new and I know little.

So I am assuming that you have some sort of a system to separate the different growth stages. From my understanding, they need to be seperate or they eat each other. Beetles on the top, eggs, then meal worms on the bottom. Then, you have to seperate the larve when they show up. The best thing I have seen that separates the larve from the worms is a salad spinner insert. You want it to have long-ish holes that are too narrow for the larve but will let the mealworms pass through. Space coast mealworms has a sifter like this but it is like 60 bucks... no thanks...

So after a lot of shaking, I drilled an old sawsall bit and attached it to a piece of roofing metal. You could use any type of jigsaw or something similar. Then, I cut a big hole in the metal that was the size of my colander(s)

And shake! I rest the contraption on a bin so it can move freely. Sift the worms out of the eggs- no problem. Sift the larve out of the worms, no problem. It is a little harder to get the worms out of the beetles ( that happens sometimes) but you can let them migrate from a colander with round holes.

I have been doing this since about June and am pretty happy with how it has been going. They are multiplying which is great.

The big industrial farms have shaker methods, much more advanced than my saw, but this does a good job for my needs. I have about 50ish chickens so mealworms is the biggest expense.

The contraption I made uses screen mesh stapled tightly about a 1"*2" in a rectangle frame cut to fit the bottom cut out of a Tupperware, screwed in to attach. The beetles burrow to the bottom of that and lay their eggs on the mesh which then fall into the deeper Tupperware which the breeding chamber seats. There are oats in the bottom for them to feed upon and air holes drilled around the bottom perimeter of the breeding chamber. No shaking or sorting required.
